2
J U D G M E N T
DIPANKAR DATTA, J.
I. INTRODUCTION
1. On the tip of Switzerland, sharing its borders with France and
Germany, lies the city of Basel. Through this city runs the river Rhine.
As the river winds through the city, the Bank for International
Settlements (BIS), a pivotal institution at the heart of the global
financial system, stands prominently on its bank.
2. In or about 2008, a certain bank - the term used loosely at this
juncture - collapsed. What followed therefrom led to a series of one
of the biggest financial meltdowns in history, ripples of which were felt
across the world. This led to, among other things, the enactment in
2010 of the Basel III Capital Regulations or the Basel III framework by
the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision at the BIS. The Reserve
Bank of India1 has implemented this framework through its Master
Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations2
.
3. The present judgment interprets parts of the RBI's mammoth Master
Circular-possibly, the first of its kind by this Court to date. The novelty
of this decision is less of a fascination and more of a formidable
challenge, as we are mindful of the large-scale impact it may have,
both immediate and gradual. Over the course of the last few decades,
the banking and finance industry has ballooned into a sector worth
1 RBI
2 Master Circular

3
billions. To a large extent, the RBI regulates this space. Its rules,
regulations, and guidelines are routinely subjected to interpretation by
law firms, senior advocates, retired judges and the like. Seldom do
these disputes reach this Court. This leads to challenges in judicial
clarity over matters of fiscal nature. Keeping all of this in mind, we now
approach the matter at hand.
II. THE FACTS
4. A judgment and order dated 20th January, 20233
, passed by the High
Court of Judicature at Bombay4
is impugned before us. The impugned
order succinctly records the detailed factual matrix; to avoid prolixity,
we advert only to a few dates that are relevant to the analysis which
follows.
5. On 23rd December, 2016, Yes Bank Limited5
issued Basel III Compliant
Additional Tier I Bonds6
in the form of non-convertible debentures for
Rs. 3,000 crore. On 18th October, 2017, a further tranche of AT-1 Bonds
was issued for Rs. 5,415 crore. For both sets of AT-1 Bonds, Axis
Trustee Services Limited7 was appointed as the trustee company. The
AT-1 Bonds were regulated by the Master Circular.
6. Since the financial position of YES BANK underwent a steep decline, on
5
th March, 2020, the Central Government imposed a moratorium on it
under section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 19498
till 3rd April,
3
impugned order
4 High Court
5 YES BANK
6 AT-1 Bonds or Bonds, used interchangeably
7 Axis Trustee
8 BR Act

4
2020. On the same day, a notification under section 36ACA of the BR
Act came to be issued by the RBI appointing an Administrator in
supersession of the Board of Directors of YES BANK and to oversee it.
On the day following, 6
th March, 2020 to be precise, a draft scheme9
of reconstruction of YES BANK was placed in the public domain and
comments were invited from the general public by 9th March, 2020.
Objections were duly lodged.
7. On 13th March, 2020, the Central Government notified the final
reconstruction scheme called the 'Yes Bank Limited Reconstruction
Scheme, 2020'
10. The Reconstruction Scheme, in its final form,
underwent certain changes from the Draft Scheme, which we propose
to deal with at a later part of this judgment.
8. On 14th March, 2020, the Administrator wrote down the AT-1 Bonds.
This was also communicated to the Bombay Stock Exchange11 and the
National Stock Exchange12
. While there is a substantial difference
between the words 'write off' and 'write down' as per the Master
Circular, throughout our reasoning, we would refer to the
Administrator's act as writing down since those are the very words
used in his letter dated 14th March, 2020.
9. It was this act of writing down of the AT-1 Bonds by the Administrator
on 14th March, 2020 which was impugned in several writ petitions
9 Draft Scheme
10 Reconstruction Scheme
11 BSE
12 NSE

5
before the High Court. While allowing the challenge, the High Court set
aside the Administrator's action.
III. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THIS COURT
10. Hearings on these appeals have spanned over several days, with
several versions and iterations of written notes and submissions,
compilations of documents and precedents being filed before and after
the hearing concluded. Several senior counsel and counsel were heard
by us at considerable length.
11. Notably, we have heard the erudite arguments of the Solicitor General
of India, Mr. Tushar Mehta for the RBI and the State Bank of India13
,
and learned senior counsel Mr. Shyam Divan and Mr. Balbir Singh for
YES BANK and its Administrator, respectively, who assailed the
impugned judgment urging various grounds. We have also heard
equally erudite arguments from learned senior counsel, viz. Mr. C.A.
Sundaram, Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, and Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul,
and other counsel appearing for the respondents, as well as the party-in-person Mr. L.V. Srinivasan who, joining online, sought to sustain the
impugned judgment.
IV. ANALYSIS
12. The issues arising for our consideration are:
A. Whether, in view of developments subsequent to the writing down
of the AT-1 Bonds, a decision on merits is unwarranted?
13 SBI

6
B. Whether the Administrator could write down the AT-1 Bonds in the
absence of a specific provision in the Reconstruction Scheme?
C. Whether the act of the Administrator in writing down the AT-1 Bonds
was in consonance with the Master Circular and the terms of the
Information Memorandum of the AT-1 Bonds?
ISSUE A: WRITING DOWN AND ITS FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
13. Appellants contend that if the impugned judgment is allowed to stand,
it would trigger a severe financial avalanche; not just for YES BANK but
for the entire banking system, undoing the very reconstruction
exercise meant to lift YES BANK out of the financial crisis it faced.
14. Respondents, conversely, contend that YES BANK's financial position has
since risen well above regulatory levels, and that the impugned
judgment - which struck down the Administrator's decision to write
down the AT-1 Bonds - should therefore be sustained. After SBI
infused funds under the Reconstruction Scheme, YES BANK's share price
rose; and once the Scheme's three-year lock-in period expired, SBI
sold its majority stake in YES BANK at a substantial profit14. All parties,
the respondents contend, have gained from the exercise.
15. The issue does not brook a short-cut; hence, we do not propose to end
the lis by simply taking note of events subsequent to the impugned
judgment and close the matter. We are reminded of a decision of this
Court in Yash Deep Trexim Private Limited v. Namokar Vinimay
14 While no document recording the sale has been placed on record, we have simply noted
the submission.

7
Pvt. Ltd.15 where this Court left the short but precise legal question16
open for decision in an appropriate case without, perhaps, foreseeing
that such an appropriate case may never arise again. Be that as it may,
the lis which unfolds before us calls for a resolution taking into
consideration the position and circumstances that stood on the date
when the Administrator ordered the AT-1 Bonds to be written down,
i.e., on 14th March, 2020. Trite it is, in cases of challenge to an
administrative action, the validity of such action must be tested as it
existed on the date on which it took place, in view of the law as it stood
then. Subsequent actions, inaction, or change in circumstances, that
affect the impugned decision cannot and ought not to have an effect
on the outcome of the lis raised in the writ petition. To this extent, we
are fortified by the view taken by this Court in Nawabkhan
Abbaskhan v. State of Gujarat17
.
16. As noted, the respondents before us challenged the validity of the
Administrator's action in several writ petitions presented before the
High Court. The High Court was tasked to examine the validity of such
action as it stood on the day when the order of writing down the AT-1
Bonds was passed. The High Court did so and struck down the
Administrator's order. We too, therefore, wish to examine it in view of
the facts and the law as it stood as on date.
15 (2014) 1 SCC 545
16 Whether the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act is applicable to foreign
companies registered in India under Section 591 of the Companies Act, 1956?
17 (1974) 2 SCC 121

8
ISSUE B: THE DRAFT SCHEME, THE RECONSTRUCTION SCHEME, AND THE
ADMINISTRATOR'S AUTHORITY
17. The primary ground urged by the respondents and accepting which the
High Court vide the impugned judgment allowed the writ petitions, was
that the Reconstruction Scheme did away with the clause providing for
the writing down of the AT-1 Bonds. In the absence of a specific clause
authorising the Administrator to write down the Bonds - and given, in
particular, the Central Government's deletion of the clause that had
provided for such a write down - the Administrator's action fell afoul
of the Reconstruction Scheme.
18. In order to appreciate this contention, we reproduce the relevant
provisions of the BR Act, the relevant clauses of the Draft Scheme and
the Reconstruction Scheme, and the events that took place between
6
th March, 2020 and 13th March, 2020.
19. YES BANK was reconstituted/reconstructed - the word 'reconstituted'
having been amended to 'reconstructed' by the Banking Regulation
(Amendment) Act, 2020 - under the provisions of section 45 of the
BR Act.
20. Clause 6 of the Draft Scheme read thus:
6. Rights and liabilities of the Reconstructed Bank:
Unless otherwise expressly provided in the scheme, all contracts, deeds,
bonds, agreements, powers of attorney, grants of legal representation
and other instruments of whatever nature, subsisting or having effect
immediately before the Appointed date, shall be effective to the extent
and in the same manner, as was applicable before the Scheme.
It shall not be necessary to obtain the consent of any third party or other
person who is a party to any of the aforesaid instruments or arrangements
to give effect to them.
All the deposits with and liabilities of the Reconstructed bank, except as
provided in the scheme, and the rights, liabilities and obligations of its

9
creditors, will continue in the same manner and with the same terms and
conditions, completely unaffected by this Scheme.
The instruments qualifying as Additional Tier 1 capital, issued by the YES
BANK Ltd. under Basel III framework, shall stand written down
permanently, in full, with effect from the Appointed date. This is in
conformity with the extant regulations issued by Reserve Bank of India
based on the Basel framework.
No accountholder shall be entitled to get any compensation from the
Reconstructed bank on account of the changes occurred in the
Reconstructed bank by virtue of the Scheme.
Any cause of action accrued, suit, appeal or other proceeding of whatever
nature pending, and decree or recovery certificate obtained by or against
the Reconstructed bank, will remain unaffected by the Scheme.
(emphasis supplied by learned senior counsel for the respondents)
21. The corresponding clause of the Reconstruction Scheme reads thus:
6. Rights and liabilities of the Reconstructed Bank:
(1) Unless otherwise expressly provided in this scheme, all contracts,
deeds, bonds, agreements, powers of attorney, grants of legal
representation and other instruments of whatever nature, subsisting or
having effect immediately before the commencement of this Scheme,
shall be effective to the extent and in the same manner, as was applicable
before such commencement.
(2) It shall not be necessary to obtain the consent of any third party or
other person who is a party to any of the aforesaid instruments or
arrangements to give effect to them.
(3) All the deposits with and liabilities of the reconstructed bank, except
as provided in this Scheme, and the rights, liabilities and obligations of
its creditors, shall continue in the same manner and with the same terms
and conditions, completely unaffected by this Scheme.
(4) No person shall be entitled to get any compensation from the
Reconstructed bank on account of the changes in the reconstructed bank
by virtue of this Scheme.
(5) Any cause of action accrued, suit, appeal or other proceeding of
whatever nature pending, and decree or recovery certificate obtained by
or against the reconstructed bank, will remain unaffected by this Scheme.
(emphasis supplied by learned senior counsel for the appellants)
22. A juxtaposition of the two clauses reveals a conspicuous absence: what
would otherwise have been sub-clause (4) of clause 6 is missing from
the Reconstruction Scheme. The paragraph providing that the AT-1
Bonds would be written down in full was omitted.
23. Certain events occurred before the moratorium was imposed on 5th
March, 2020 as well as between the publication of the Draft Scheme
and the publication of the Reconstruction Scheme; we notice these,

10
hereafter, both to ascertain whether they were at all relevant and, if
so, to what extent.
24. Several stakeholders, including the primary stakeholder Axis Trustee
(respondent no. 1), wrote to YES BANK Limited a day before the
moratorium was imposed, i.e., on 4th March, 2020, expressing concern
about its functioning and apprehension that the bondholders' interests
could be prejudiced. Axis Trustee requested a face-to-face meeting
with YES BANK's senior management within twenty-four hours.
25. Likewise, Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited18, an investor in the AT-1
Bonds, also wrote to YES BANK on 3rd March, 2020, requiring it, inter
alia, to redeem all the AT-1 Bonds and not to write them down.
26. After the Draft Scheme was published, Axis Trustee, on 8th March,
2020, voiced concerns over the proposed write down on behalf of
various institutional and retail bondholders. Inter alia, Axis Trustee
raised the delayed announcement of financial results for the quarter
ended December 2019, and its effect on the AT-1 Bonds, and pleaded
that the bonds be converted into equity instead.
27. Around the same time, IHFL also wrote to the RBI opposing the Draft
Scheme's proposal to write down the AT-1 Bonds.
28. Before the Reconstruction Scheme could be notified, Axis Trustee had
already filed a writ petition19 before the High Court. Pursuant to that
petition, Axis Trustee wrote to the RBI again, on 11th March, 2020,
calling for the bonds to be converted to equity instead of being written
18 IHFL
19 the writ petition having been later disposed of by a separate order, neither the petition
nor the order has been placed on record.

11
down entirely, and undertook that should the RBI adopt this course, it
would withdraw the petition.
29. At this juncture, an internal note20 submitted by the RBI to the
Department of Financial Services, Government of India (subsequently
obtained through the mechanism of the Right to Information Act,
2005) becomes relevant. The Note was circulated to seek the approval
of the Union Finance Minister and the Cabinet, and records that, after
publication of the Draft Scheme, the RBI received comments from
individuals and investors expressing concern in regard to the writing
down of the AT-1 Bonds. These observations appear at paragraph 3.4.6
of the Note. Given the reliance placed on it by all the parties, we set
out the relevant portion verbatim as under:
AT1 bonds
3.4.6. With regard on AT1 bonds, RBI has stated that the bank has issued
three series of AT1 bonds at different points of time as under:
ISIN Amount (in
crore Rs.)
Issue date Coupon
1 INE528G08261 280.00 31.12.2013 10.5%
2 INE528G08352 3,000.00 23.12.2016 9.5%
3 INE528G08394 5,415.00 18.10.2017 9.0%
TOTAL 8,695.00
3.4.6.1 RBI has stated that it is pertinent to note that in the first series of
Rs. 280 crore, a clause has been included in the term-sheet under which
the bonds can be written down on the occurrence of loss-absorption events
only after the common equity capital has been written down. Since bonds
of this series are not Basel-III compliant instruments, these have not been
reckoned for the purpose of write down or conversion in the scheme. The
second bond series, aggregating Rs. 3,000 crore, provides for write-down
and conversion at both the pre-specified trigger level and point of non-viability (PONV). The terms of the third bond, aggregating Rs. 5,415 crore,
provide for only write-down at both the triggers.
20 F. No. 7/19/2020-BOA.I: the Note hereafter

12
3.4.6.2 RBI guidelines contained in Annex 16 of RBI's Master Circular on
Basel III Capital Regulations, 2015 state as under.
(a) Paragraph 2.3: Write-down of common equity tier I capital shall
not be required before a write-down of any AT1 capital.
(b) Paragraph 2.15: If relevant authorities decide to reconstitute a
bank or amalgamate a bank with any other bank under section 45 of
B. R. Act, such a bank will be deemed as non-viable or approaching
nonviability and both the pre-specified trigger and trigger at PONV
for conversion/write-down of AT1 instruments will be activated.
Accordingly, AT1 instruments will be fully converted or Written down
permanently before amalgamation/reconstitution in accordance with
the rules. In case of reconstitution or amalgamation of banking
company under section 45 ibid, at PONV, conversion or write-down
of AT1 instruments will be activated and such conversion/write down
will be before amalgamation or reconstitution of the bank.
(c) Paragraph 3.1: In case of PONV trigger, write-off of any CET1
capital shall not be required before write-off of any non-equity (AT1
and Tier 2) regulatory capital instrument.
3.4.6.3 RBI has stated that it is thus very clear from the above that as per
RBI guidelines on Basel III capital regulations, write-off/conversion of AT1
capital has to happen before write-off of CET1 capital. RBI has further stated
that it is seen that the term-sheet of AT1 bonds provide multiple options
providing 'only write down' or 'conversion or write down', which could lead
to possible litigation. To prevent any present and future litigation, the bond
trustee of AT-1 bonds has proposed conversion. By this, bonds are getting
converted at Rs. 51, which is close to the share price as per the SEBI (Listing
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 ("LODR")
formula for preferential allotment as per SEBI rules. Effectively, because of
new investors, as the other investors participating in the scheme are being
allotted equity shares at Rs. 10 per share, allotting 1.955 per share per Rs.
100 will tantamount to AT1 bondholders getting 20% value of their
investment with possibilities for future upside.
3.4.6.3.1 With regard to treatment of AT-1 bonds, the extant
guidelines/rules/ regulations of RBI and bond conditions apply. Therefore,
it may not be appropriate to modify these through the proposed
Reconstruction Scheme. Accordingly, related provision in the draft scheme
furnished by RBI may be dropped.
(emphasis ours, by underlining)
30. The Note also took into consideration the pending litigation concerning
the AT-1 bonds. Its observations, at paragraph 3.4.10, read as under:
Writ petition filed by Axis Trustee Services Limited
3.4.10 RBI has informed that that it has received a notice of filing of a writ
petition in Bombay High Court by Axis Trustee Services Limited on
9.3.2020, vide which the petitioner has prayed-
(a) To issue direction to RBI to give an effective opportunity to the
petitioner to make a detailed representation, incorporating

13
reservations, objections and suggestions to RBI on the draft scheme,
and to provide an opportunity of hearing and audience on its
representation;
(b) To pass an order refraining RBI and Union of India from
implementing the scheme, until the petitioner is given a hearing and
audience by the respondent, and consider the representation of the
petitioner; and
(c) To restrain RBI from implementing the scheme to the extent that
the said scheme purports to write off, permanently, in full, the
debenture issued to the petitioner under Debenture Trusts Deed
dated 15.3.2017 and 28.12.2017 respectively; pending hearing and
disposal of the present petition, the court may restrain RBI in
implementing the scheme.
3.4.10.1 RBI has informed that the matter was to be heard on 11.3.2020,
but no hearing took place and that it is not listed for any further date. The
petitioner has requested RBI that the matter being sub-judice, RBI should
not precipitate any action to the prejudice of the AT1 bondholders. RBI has
stated that, however, as at the time of sending of this letter, there is no
stay granted by the Court on the scheme, and that RBI is forwarding the
final draft of the scheme to the Central Government for sanction and
notification.
3.4.10.2 RBI has stated that it may be observed that the petitioner had
already submitted its detailed comments/suggestions on the draft 'YES BANK
Reconstruction Scheme-2020', vide email dated 8.3.2020 and, as
mentioned earlier, all the comments received from various quarters have
been duly analysed and appropriate action taken. These comments include
the comments submitted by Axis Trustee Services Ltd. Further, wide
(sic vide) letter dated 11.3.2020, Axis Trustee Services Ltd (the petitioner),
which is acting as trustee for the Basel-III bonds, has stated that majority
bondholders (three fourth) of AT1 bonds are agreeable that upon
notification of the final Scheme of reconstruction of the bank, the AT-1
bonds shall stand fully converted on the basis of a conversion ratio of
19,551 equity shores (sic) of Rs. 2 each of the reconstructed bank to be
issued for each AT-1 Bond with a face value of Rs. 10,00,000. Accordingly,
shares shall be allotted to the existing AT1 holders in proportion to their
current holding of these bonds. RBI has informed that the suggestion has
suitably been considered and incorporated in the revised Reconstruction
Scheme.
31. The final clause of the Note, which summarises the salient features of
the proposed Reconstruction Scheme, reads thus:
Final draft of the Reconstruction Scheme
3.4.12 Against this background, RBI has placed the final draft of the "YES
BANK Ltd. Reconstruction Scheme, 2020" ("Reconstruction Scheme")
[pp. 279-184/c] for sanction and notification.
3.4.12.1 Salient features of the proposed Reconstruction Scheme are as
under:

14
...
(q) The Basel III compliant AT-1 bonds issued by the reconstructed bank
shall stand fully converted on the basis of a conversion ratio of 19,551
equity shares of Rs. 2 each of the reconstructed bank to be issued for each
AT-1 Bond with a face value of Rs. 10,00,000. Accordingly, share shall be
allotted to the existing Basel III compliant AT-1 bond holders in proportion
to their current holding of these bonds.
32. Approval of the Union Finance Minister was sought in the following
terms:
8. Approval sought
8.1 Approval of the Finance Minister is sought for the following:
(a) The updated draft note for the Cabinet, placed below, for soliciting
approval of the Cabinet for sanction to the "YES BANK Ltd. Reconstruction
Scheme, 2020", and submitting the note for the Cabinet to the Cabinet
Secretariat with the request that the Ministry of Law and Justice may make
its views known in the meeting of the Cabinet through the Minister of Law
and Justice;
(b) In the event of Cabinet according approval to the proposed scheme by
13.3.2020, keeping in view RBI's communication that it would prefer that
the Reconstruction Scheme is notified on 13.3.2020, to notify the said date
as the appointed date for the scheme; and
(c) In the event of Cabinet according approval to the proposed scheme,
issuing on the same date the notification recommended by RBI under
section 53 of B.R. Act, for exempting State Bank of India (SBI) from the
application of the provision of section 19(2) ibid. insofar as they relate to
the holding of shares of SBI in YES BANK Ltd., for a period of four years from
the date of notification.
33. On 13th March, 2020, the Reconstruction Scheme was published in the
Official Gazette21, with the clause as set out in paragraph 21
hereinabove. On the next day, 14th March, 2020, the Administrator
wrote down the AT-1 Bonds which was impugned in the writ petitions
before the High Court.
34. Two material observations, of relevance, emerge from these events:
(a) the cognizance taken by the RBI of the comments and suggestions
21 Gazette

15
submitted by various stakeholders, as revealed by the Note; and (b)
the complete absence, from the Reconstruction Scheme, of the clause
providing for the writing down of the AT-1 Bonds.
35. Both these events, considered together, lift the curtain on the reasons
and deliberation that took place which crystallised into the finally
approved Reconstruction Scheme. The RBI and the Central
Government noticed the concerns and the apprehensions raised by the
investors. Having done so, the Note reflects that substantial changes
were made to the Draft Scheme. The suggestion of the primary
stakeholder, viz. Axis Trustee, that the bonds may be converted into
equity was also taken into consideration and necessary changes were
suggested.
36. A crucial fact that has remained inconspicuous is the writ petition filed
soon after the Draft Scheme was published. The Note records that a
majority of investors had agreed to conversion of the bonds into equity
shares - Rs. 2 each, for each bond of face value Rs. 10,00,000.00 -
a proposal the RBI accepted as presented by Axis Trustee, acting in a
fiduciary capacity on behalf of the bondholders.
37. For reasons undisclosed but of little relevance, the proposal to write
down or convert the bonds was abandoned in its entirety at the stage
when the scheme was considered by the Central Government. It would
necessarily follow, in the entire deliberative process, that the Central
Government thought it fit not to tinker with the bonds at all through
the Reconstruction Scheme. While it remains a matter of speculation,

16
it appears the intent was to avoid the pending litigation concerning the
bonds, which had already been instituted.
38. It would not be out of place to presume that the Central Government
was well aware of the direct effect on the Common Equity Tier 1 ratio
of not writing down or converting the bonds in the Reconstruction
Scheme. By consciously choosing not to incorporate any clause in the
Reconstruction Scheme that would affect the bonds, the Central
Government thus gave its imprimatur to leaving it untouched.
39. For the Administrator to then turn volte-face the decision of the Central
Government by writing down the AT-1 Bonds entirely, did away with
the deliberative process that occurred between the Draft Scheme and
the Reconstruction Scheme. After the Reconstruction Scheme having
been notified on 13th March, 2020, the understanding would be that
YES BANK stood reconstituted/reconstructed in its entirety. It was viable
enough to continue surviving as a banking institution. It would be
unreasonable to infer that the RBI and the Central Government would
undertake the entirety of a long-drawn process of crafting the
Reconstruction Scheme and seemingly leave out the crucial part
concerning the AT-1 Bonds. If the appellants' arguments were to be
accepted, the Reconstruction Scheme would be akin to a half-baked
pie, where the last step of the process is left to the Administrator.
40. Even otherwise, we are afraid, accepting the argument that the
authority of the Administrator under the Reconstruction Scheme to
write down the AT-1 Bonds was retained would have its own
ramifications. We have good reasons to infer that the Central

17
Government had taken a conscious decision to exclude the clause
permitting writing down of the AT-1 Bonds from the Reconstruction
Scheme, based on consideration of the objections lodged. If it were
the intention of the Central Government to allow the Administrator to
write down the AT-1 Bonds after publication of the Reconstruction
Scheme even after exclusion of the relevant clause from the Draft
Scheme, that would have made it susceptible to face the criticism of
acting clandestinely and the accusation of committing an act
amounting to a fraud on public. We do not, for a moment, think that
the Central Government intended to have the AT-1 Bonds written
down, having regard to the turn of events right from 3rd March, 2020.
Instead, it happened to be the Administrator who, in our opinion, acted
under an erroneous impression or mistaken belief that reconstruction
of YES BANK by virtue of the Reconstruction Scheme notwithstanding,
he retained the authority to write down the AT-1 Bonds. This, in our
opinion, was an impermissible act and ultra vires the Master Circular
read with the Reconstruction Scheme.
41. Before parting with this segment of the discussion, we place on record
reliance placed by Mr. Divan and Mr. Singh upon sub-clause (1) of
clause 6 of the Reconstruction Scheme which sought to preserve the
efficacy of the bonds in the same manner before its commencement.
They further contended that the Reconstruction Scheme did not
abrogate the Administrator's inherent power to execute a write-down
of the AT-1 Bonds. While it is true that the Administrator's residuary
powers are preserved under the aforementioned clause, such a general

18
savings provision does not, by itself, confer the specific authority to
write down the AT-1 Bonds after YES BANK came to be reconstructed. A
definitive mechanism governing the treatment of AT-1 Bonds is
prescribed by the Master Circular and the respective Information
Memoranda, stipulating a separate and distinct procedural framework
for each issuance in strict conformity with the Master Circular. It is a
settled legal principle that a power not specifically conferred cannot be
implicitly vested through a general, omnibus savings clause. To that
extent, we rule against YES BANK and the Administrator.
42. Thus, the High Court correctly held that the Administrator could not
have written down the Bonds in contravention of the Reconstruction
Scheme.
ISSUE C: THE MASTER CIRCULAR, THE INFORMATION MEMORANDA AND THE
ADMINISTRATOR'S ACT OF WRITING DOWN THE AT-1 BONDS
43. It has been contended by all the appellants that notwithstanding the
finally published Reconstruction Scheme, the Administrator was always
empowered to write down the AT-1 Bonds. The specific contention of
the appellants was that the Administrator acting under Section 36ACA
of the BR Act and under the Information Memoranda of the AT-1 Bonds
was empowered to write them down, in terms of the conditions
stipulated therein. It was further contended that even if the
Reconstruction Scheme did not provide for writing down the bonds,
that in itself would not preclude the Administrator from exercising such
power.

19
44. We proceed to consider this issue unaffected by the outcome of the
part discussed before, which is unfavourable to the appellants.
45. The contention raised must be examined from two perspectives: first,
the conditions that empowered the Administrator to write down the
bonds; and secondly, whether the conditions that were required to be
satisfied in the exercise of such power. To do so, we first examine the
Master Circular and the Information Memorandum to the extent
relevant for the present purpose.
46. The Master Circular, under paragraph 4, divides regulatory capital of a
bank in 2 parts: Tier 1 Capital and Tier 2 Capital. Tier 1 Capital is
termed as the 'going-concern capital', whereas Tier 2 Capital is termed
'gone-concern capital'. As is self-explanatory, going-concern capital
can absorb losses without triggering a bank's insolvency, whereas
gone-concern capital absorbs losses in the event of the bank's
liquidation.
47. Tier 1 Capital is further divided into Common Equity Tier 122 and
Additional Tier 123. Under the Master Circular, a bank must maintain
total Tier 1 Capital equal to at least 7% of its Risk Weighted Assets
(RWAs). Of this, at least 5.5% must be in the form of CET1. What
constitutes CET 1 Capital is provided in clause 4.2.3 of the Master
Circular read with Annex 1 thereof. The remaining 1.5% may,
optionally, be met through AT1 Capital; which means that a bank is
22 CET1
23 AT1

20
not required to have any AT1 Capital at all and may choose to meet
the entire 7% requirement through CET1 alone.
48. AT1 capital may be issued in various forms, such as Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares (PNCPS) or debt capital instruments, as
in the present case. As long as an instrument complies with the
conditions stipulated for it in the Master Circular, it can be reckoned
towards AT1 capital. Here, Annex 4 of the Master Circular provides the
criteria for issuance of the bonds.
49. Annex 16 of the Master Circular has been extensively relied upon by
counsel for the parties; for that reason, we examine its components at
this juncture.
50. Annex 16 provides the loss absorbency feature of the AT1 instruments.
It further specifies two trigger events at which the loss absorbency
feature may be exercised viz. (i) Pre-Specified Trigger Level; and (ii)
Point of Non-Viability.
51. As per clause 2 of Annex 16, the Pre-Specified Trigger Level is reached
when a bank's CET1 ratio falls below 6.125% of RWA (in case of YES
BANK, 5.5% before 31st March, 2019, and 6.125% on or after that date,
as per the Information Memorandum). This 6.125% threshold
comprises the minimum CET1 requirement (5.5%) plus 25% of the
capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, i.e., 0.625%.
52. Thus, the moment YES BANK's CET1 ratio fell below the threshold of
6.125%, YES BANK had the option to convert or write down the AT1
instruments.

21
53. The unaudited financial results for the third quarter and nine months
ended 31st December, 2019 were considered and taken on record by
the Administrator on 14th March, 2020, and intimated to the BSE and
the NSE. It may be noted that the publication of reports in terms of
SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations,
2015 was delayed even before the Administrator took charge. A
perusal of the accompanying statement by the auditor reveals that as
on 31st December, 2019, about 2 months prior to the moratorium and
the Reconstruction Scheme, the CET1 ratio stood at an astonishing
0.6% as against a requirement of 7.375%.
54. Thus, despite having the option but not the obligation to convert or
write down the bonds, YES BANK chose not to. We do not intend to
question such wisdom.
55. Instead, attempt was made to raise further capital. Having failed to do
so, the Central Government intervened and imposed a moratorium on
5
th March, 2020, and the RBI appointed the Administrator under
section 36ACA of the BR Act. The Draft Scheme was published the
following day.
56. After the Reconstruction Scheme came to be published in the Gazette
following the statutory procedure, the Administrator decided to write
down the bonds in its entirety. The reasons given by the Administrator
for writing down the bonds, as recorded in his order, read thus:
B) Position under RBI regulations
1) As per the provisions of the Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations
dated July 1, 2015 issued by the RBI, ("Basel III Circular"), more
specifically, clause 2.15 of Annex 16 of the Basel III Circular,

22
"If the relevant authorities decide to reconstitute a bank or amalgamate a
bank with any other bank under the Section 45 of BR Act, 1949, such a
bank will be deemed as non-viable or approaching non- viability and both
the pre-specified trigger and the trigger at the point of non-viability for
conversion /write-down of AT 1 Instruments will be activated. Accordingly,
the AT1 instruments will be fully converted/written-down permanently
before amalgamation/reconstitution in accordance with these rules"
2) Given that Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 has been
invoked by the RBI and the Scheme has been notified, the Bank is deemed
to be non-viable or approaching non-viability and accordingly, the triggers
for a write-down of the AT 1 Bonds has been triggered. Such AT 1 Bonds
would need to be fully written down permanently before any reconstruction
of the Bank is undertaken.
In light of the above provisions of the Basel III Circular, it is hereby ordered
that the Perpetual Subordinated Basel III Compliant Additional Tier I Bonds
issued by the Bank for an amount of Rs. 3000 crores on December 23, 2016
and the Perpetual Subordinated Basel III Compliant Additional Tier 1 Bonds
issued by the Bank for an amount of Rs. 5415 crores on October 18, 2017
be fully written down and shall stand extinguished with immediate effect.
57. Mr. Divan and Mr. Singh have strenuously contended that, under the
Master Circular, the publication of the Reconstruction Scheme in the
Gazette both triggered that write down as well as empowered the
Administrator to write down the AT-1 Bonds.
58. Per contra, much emphasis has been placed by the respondents on
clause 2.15 of the Master Circular and particularly on the phrase
'before reconstitution' therein.
59. It would, thus be profitable to read what the Master Circular provides
in relation to schemes of amalgamation and reconstruction. The
relevant clause reads as under:
(a) Amalgamation of a banking company: (Section 44 A of BR Act, 1949)
2.12 If a bank is amalgamated with any other bank before the AT1
instruments have been written-down/converted, these instruments will
become part of the corresponding categories of regulatory capital of the
new bank emerging after the merger.
2.13 If a bank is amalgamated with any other bank after the AT1
instruments have been written down temporarily, the amalgamated entity
can write-up these instruments as per its discretion.

23
2.14 If a bank is amalgamated with any other bank after the non-equity
regulatory capital instruments have been written-down permanently, these
cannot be written-up by the amalgamated entity.
(b) Scheme of reconstitution or amalgamation of a banking company:
(Section 45 of BR Act, 1949)
2.15 If the relevant authorities decide to reconstitute a bank or amalgamate
a bank with any other bank under the Section 45 of BR Act, 1949, such a
bank will be deemed as non-viable or approaching non-viability and both
the pre-specified trigger and the trigger at the point of nonviability for
conversion / write-down of AT1 instruments will be activated. Accordingly,
the AT1 instruments will be fully converted / written-down permanently
before amalgamation / reconstitution in accordance with these rules.
(emphasis ours)
60. To interpret the phrase 'before reconstitution', reliance has been placed
on clause 1 and clause 2(1)(d) of the Reconstruction Scheme, which
read thus:
1. Short title and commencement - (1) This Scheme may be called the Yes
Bank Limited Reconstruction Scheme, 2020.
(2) it shall come into force on the 13th day of March, 2020.
2. Definitions. (1) In this Scheme, unless the context otherwise requires-
...
d) "reconstructed bank" means the YES BANK Limited, a banking company
having its registered office at YES BANK Tower, IFC-2, 15th Floor, Prabhadevi
(W), Mumbai-400013, Maharashtra;
61. The definition of 'reconstructed bank' was pressed upon us, repeatedly,
by learned senior counsel for the appellants to contend that the
reconstruction process of YES BANK did not start until the
Reconstruction Scheme was published in the Gazette, and that the
right to write down the AT-1 Bonds arose only thereafter. Responding
to our query as to when would the reconstruction exercise stand
completed, the answer given was: not until every obligation under the
Reconstruction Scheme had been discharged - meaning the exercise
would continue until the last act under the Reconstruction Scheme was

24
performed, which might well be three years after the Scheme's
notification.
62. Relying on the definition of a 'reconstructed bank', Mr. Divan submitted
that reconstruction of the reconstructed bank is a continuous process
in terms of the Reconstruction Scheme. The contention advanced was
that the reconstruction process did not commence until the
Reconstruction Scheme was published in the Gazette, and more
crucially, it remains ongoing until every obligation under the Scheme
is completely discharged. On this premise, it was argued that the
power to write down the AT-1 Bonds would continue to subsist with the
Administrator until such time the reconstructed bank is fully
reconstructed.
63. This part of the controversy turns on an incorrect interpretation of
Clause 2.15 of Annex 16 of the Master Circular. The trigger viz. the
point of non-viability is deemed to have been reached when the
relevant authorities decide to reconstruct YES BANK, and in such an
event the AT-1 Bonds ought to have been written down before the
initial step of the reconstitution/reconstruction happened, i.e., the
Reconstruction Scheme came into force. The preposition 'before' can
only mean before the Reconstruction Scheme takes effect. True, the
effects of a reconstruction scheme may run for years together; but
that, by itself, cannot be read as empowering the relevant authority to
write down the AT-1 Bonds at any point within the following three
years. Had the intention been otherwise, the clause ought to have read
"before reconstitution is complete". We cannot by taking the aid of any

25
tool of interpretation read words in the relevant clause which are
conspicuous by its absence. To read the clause in its present form in
the manner urged by Mr. Divan would not only defeat the very object
of the AT-1 Bonds but would produce an inherent absurdity, leaving
investors to wonder at what point the guillotine blade might fall.
64. History bears this out. In the counter-affidavit filed by one of the
respondents, i.e., 63 Moons Technologies Limited, a similar scenario
involving a pari materia clause has been placed on record. Lakshmi
Vilas Bank Limited was amalgamated with DBS Bank India Limited,
and the information memorandum for its bonds - Basel III compliant
Tier 2 Bonds - contained a similar clause, activating the trigger for
writing down the bonds upon amalgamation / reconstitution. The
amalgamation scheme was published in the Gazette on 25th November,
2020, and was due to come into force on 27th November, 2020. The
bonds worth Rs. 318.20 crore were written down by the administrator
in that case on 26th November, 2020, a day ahead of the amalgamation
scheme coming into force - in other words, before the amalgamation
took effect. Why the same course was not adopted remains
unexplained.
65. Another issue which must be considered is the Administrator's
authority under the Master Circular and the Information Memoranda
to write down the Bonds.
66. Clause 2.15 of Annex 16 of the Master Circular states that the point of
non-viability would be deemed to have been triggered and,
accordingly, the AT-1 Bonds would have to be converted or written

26
down in accordance with the rules. We examine both the pre-specified
trigger and the point of non-viability, as provided in the Information
Memorandum.
67. Clause 56, which provides for loss absorbency, reads as follows:
Loss absorbency:
The Bonds (including all claims, demands on the Bonds and interest
thereon, whether accrued or contingent) are issued subject to loss
absorbency features applicable for non-equity capital instruments issued in
terms of Basel III Guidelines and are subject to certain loss absorbency
features as described herein and required of Additional Tier 1 instruments
at Pre-Specified Trigger Level and at the PONV.
Accordingly, without the need of the consent of Bondholders or Trustee, the
Bonds and any claims or demands of any Bondholder or any other person
claiming for or on behalf of or through such Bondholder, against the Bank,
may be written-off, in whole or in part, upon the occurrence of the following
trigger events:
(i) Pre-Specified Trigger Level;
(ii) Point of Non-Viability.
(i) Loss Absorption at Pre-Specified Trigger Level
If the CET1 of the Bank falls below 5.5% of RWA before 31st March, 2019
and if CET1 falls below 6.125% of RWA on or after 31st March 2019. Each
of the trigger levels referred to hereinabove is called the "Pre-Specified
Trigger Level"
A write-off of the Bonds may have the following effects:
(i) reduce the claim of the Bond (up to nil) in liquidation;
(ii) reduce the amount to be re-paid on the Bond when call is exercised (up
to nil);
(iii) partially or fully reduce Coupon payments on the Bond.
The write-down of any Common Equity Tier 1 capital shall not be required
before a write-down of any AT1 instruments (including the Bonds). The
Bank shall have full discretion to determine the amount of AT1 Instruments
(including the Bonds) written down subject to the amount of write-down
not exceeding the amount which would be required to bring CET1 ratio to
8% of RWAs. Further, the aggregate amount to be written-down for all AT1
Instruments on breaching the trigger level shall be at least the amount
needed to immediately return the bank's CET1 ratio to the trigger level (i.e.
CET from write-down generated under applicable Indian Accounting
Standards or RBI Instructions net of contingent liabilities, potential tax
liabilities etc., if any) or, if this is not possible the full principal value of the
instruments. The Bank shall have the discretion to write-down the Bonds

27
multiple times in case the Bank hits Pre-Specified Trigger Level subsequent
to the first write-down. The Bonds which have been written off can be
written up (partially or full) at the absolute discretion of the Bank and
subject to compliance with RBI instructions (including permission, consent
if any).
(ii) Loss Absorption at the Point of Non-Viability ("PONV")
A write-off of the Bonds at the PONV may have the following effects:
(i) reduce the claim of the Bond (up to nil) in liquidation;
(ii) reduce the amount to be re-paid on the Bond when call is exercised (up
to nil);
iii) partially or fully reduce coupon payments on the Bond.
PONV trigger event shall be as defined in the aforesaid Basel III Guidelines
and shall be determined by the RBI.
RBI may in its imminence alter or modify the PONV trigger whether
generally or in relation to the Bank or otherwise. In any case it should be
noted that following writing-off of the Bonds and claims and demands as
noted above neither the Bank, nor any other person on the Bank's behalf
shall be required to compensate or provide any relief, whether absolutely
or contingently, to the Bondholder or any other person claiming for or on
behalf of or through such holder and all claims and demands of such
persons, whether under law, contract or equity, shall stand permanently
and irrevocably extinguished and terminated. Unless otherwise specified in
this Information Memorandum, the write-off of any common equity or any
other regulatory capital (as understood in terms of the aforesaid circular or
any replacement/amendment thereof), whether senior or pari passu or
subordinate, and whether a Tier 1 capital or otherwise shall not be required
before the write-off of any of the Bonds and there is no right available to
the Bondholder hereof or any other person claiming for or on behalf of or
through such holder to demand or seek that any other regulatory capital be
subject to prior or simultaneous write-off or that the treatment offered to
holders of such other regulatory capital be also offered to the Bondholders.
(emphasis in underline ours)
68. Clause 57, which provides for the point of non-viability, reads as
follows:
Without the need of the consent of Bondholders or Trustee, the Bonds
(including all claims, demands on the Bonds and interest thereon, whether
accrued or contingent), at the option of the RBI, can be permanently written
down upon the occurrence of the trigger event called "Point of Non-Viability
Trigger" ("PONV Trigger")
The PONV Trigger event is the earlier of:

28
(i) a decision that a permanent write-off without which the Bank would
become non-viable, as determined by the Reserve Bank of India; and
(ii) the decision to make a public sector injection of capital, or equivalent
support, without which the Bank would have become non-viable, as
determined by the relevant authority.
The amount of non-equity capital to be written-off will be determined by
RBI.
The Write-off of any Common Equity Tier 1 capital shall not be required
before the write-off of any Non-equity (Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2)
regulatory capital instrument. The order of write-off of the Bonds shall be
as specified in the order of seniority as per this Information Memorandum
and any other regulatory norms as may be stipulated by the RBI from time
to time.
The Bonds can be written-down multiple times in case the Bank hits the
PONV Trigger Level subsequent to the first write-down. The Bonds which
has been written off shall not be written up.
Such a decision would invariably imply that the write-off consequent upon
the trigger event must occur prior to any public sector injection of capital
so that the capital provided by the public sector is not diluted. The
Bondholders shall not have any residual claims on the Bank (including any
claims which are senior to ordinary shares of the Bank), following any
trigger event. In any case it should be noted that following writing-off of
the instruments and claims and demands as noted above neither the Bank,
nor any other person on the Bank's behalf shall be required to compensate
or provide any relief, whether absolutely or contingently, to the Bondholder
or any other person claiming for or on behalf of or through such holder and
all claims and demands of such persons, whether under law, contract or
equity, shall stand permanently and irrevocably extinguished and
terminated. Unless otherwise specified in this Information Memorandum,
the write-off of any common equity or any other regulatory capital (as
understood in terms of the aforesaid circular or any
replacement/amendment thereof), whether senior or pari passu or
subordinate, and whether a Tier 1 capital or otherwise shall not be required
before the write-off of any of the Bonds and there is no right available to
the Bondholder hereof or any other person claiming for or on behalf of or
through such holder to demand or seek that any other regulatory capital be
subject to prior or simultaneous write-off or that the treatment offered to
holders of such other regulatory capital be also offered to the Bondholders.
For these purposes, the Bank may be considered as non-viable if:
The Bank which, owing to its financial and other difficulties, may no longer
remain a going concern on its own in the opinion of the RBI unless
appropriate measures are taken to revive its operations and thus, enable it
to continue as a going concern. The difficulties faced by the Bank should be
such that these are likely to result in financial losses and raising the
Common Equity Tier 1 capital of the Bank should be considered as the most
appropriate way to prevent the Bank from turning non-viable. Such
measures would include write-off of non-equity regulatory capital in
combination with or without other measures as considered appropriate by
the Reserve Bank.

29
The Bank facing financial difficulties and approaching a PONV will be
deemed to achieve viability if within a reasonable time in the opinion of RBI,
it will be able to come out of the present difficulties if appropriate measures
are taken to revive it. The measures including augmentation of equity
capital through write off of Bonds/ public sector injection of funds are likely
to:
a. Restore depositors'/investors' confidence;
b. Improve rating /creditworthiness of the Bank and thereby improve its
borrowing capacity and liquidity and reduce cost of funds; and
c. Augment the resource base to fund balance sheet growth in the case of
fresh injection of funds.
The trigger at PONV will be evaluated both at consolidated and solo level
and breach at either level will trigger write-off.
(emphasis ours)
69. On a reading of clauses 56 and 57, the pre-specified trigger, as
mentioned above is reached when the CET1 ratio falls below the
specified minimum. At that threshold, the Bank may choose whether
to write off, write down, or convert the bonds, and which of the bonds
are to be treated in which way, as per the options available in the
Information Memorandum. However, once the point of non-viability is
reached, or the Bank approaches non-viability, it no longer retains that
discretion - it is then the RBI which determines, as per the standards
set out in the Master Circular, whether the Bank is approaching or has
reached the point of non-viability24, and it is then the RBI which must
write down the Bonds.

30
70. In the present case, admittedly, the point of non-viability was deemed
to have been triggered when the relevant authorities decided to
reconstruct YES BANK or even earlier. No sooner was the point of non-viability triggered than the RBI was required to write down the Bonds.
Yet it was not the RBI that decided to write down the Bonds, but the
Administrator appointed by the RBI, who wrote them down and
communicated the same to the stock exchanges. The question is
whether the Administrator can be said to have exercised the power
vested in the RBI. We hold he cannot.
71. The Administrator exercises power under section 36ACA of the BR Act,
the relevant portion of which reads as follows:
36ACA. Supersession of Board of Directors in certain cases.-

Government, that in the public interest or for preventing the affairs of any
banking company being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interest

Board of Directors of such banking company for a period not exceeding six

exceed twelve months.

who has experience in law, finance, banking, economics or accountancy.

Act, 1956 (1 of 1956),-

RBI.

31
(a) the chairman, managing director and other directors shall, as from the
date of supersession, vacate their offices as such;
(b) all the powers, functions and duties which may, by or under the

of Directors of such banking company is reconstituted, be exercised and

Provided that the power exercised by the Administrator shall be valid

(5) The Reserve Bank may constitute, in consultation with the Central

(emphasis ours)
72. Thus, an administrator appointed under the BR Act has to act squarely
within the four corners of the powers conferred upon him under the
statute. He acts as a substitute for the Board of Directors, to run the
company in an efficient manner. Any act performed by the
administrator beyond the powers clothed upon him would be wholly
illegal and void.
73. Thus, as per the Information Memorandum read with the Master
Circular, there were 2 triggers for the bonds to be written down/written
off. The first was for YES BANK to exercise; which it admittedly did not.
The second was for the RBI to exercise which, not only did it express
its intention not to-by eliminating the clause providing for writing
down-but chose not to exercise it at all. The Administrator could not
have assumed the regulatory role of the RBI and exercise a power
which it did not have at all.

32
74. Mr. Divan, in his signature tenor, attempted his best to emphasize on
the necessity of 'bail in' and 'bail out' as an integral part of the
reconstruction scheme. He contended that either of these events, by
itself, could not bring back YES BANK to life again and restore the CET1
ratio. A combined effort, first by writing down the bonds, and the
subsequent infusion of funds by SBI-the chronology being of
essence-was necessary to revive YES BANK. This submission was
adopted by Mr. Mehta.
75. It may well be true that both of these events were necessary to revive
YES BANK. However, mere necessity cannot possibly circumvent the
manner in which the write down ought to have been exercised. This
was required to be done in terms of the Master Circular only. The bail
in and bail out events merely provided a right to write down the bonds,
not the manner.
76. The pressing questions before us - to which the appellants ostensibly
proffer no answer - are these: Was SBI not aware of the Draft
Scheme, the Reconstruction Scheme, and the absence of the clause
for writing down in the Reconstruction Scheme, when it was the one
infusing funds for equity? Was the RBI, the regulator, not aware of the
consequences of not retaining the write down clause in the
Reconstruction Scheme? Was the RBI and the Administrator appointed
by the RBI not aware as to who had the authority to write down the
AT-1 Bonds as per the Master Circular? Was the Central Government
not aware that the bonds had not yet been not written down when the
Reconstruction Scheme was notified?

33
77. These questions left unanswered answer the disjunct in the entire
process carried out by the RBI, the Administrator and YES BANK. The
question is not whether the AT-1 Bonds could have been or ought to
have been written down off. The question is the manner in which it was
done, de hors the Master Circular and the Information Memoranda. A
conscious decision by the Central Government while approving the
Reconstruction Scheme by deleting the clause from the Draft Scheme,
evidently in favour of the bondholders, came to be dismantled at the
hands of the Administrator.
78. The triumvirate of the RBI, the Administrator, and of course, YES BANK,
in conducting the entire affair of dealing with the bonds worth more
than 8,514 crore is, to put it mildly, questionable. Putting the investors
to such uncalled-for risk, could have well been avoided. The purpose
of the AT-1 Bonds is imperative: it acts as a safety barrier to the Bank
from collapsing altogether. That purpose could have been served had
the RBI and YES BANK acted in accordance with the terms of the Master
Circular. The RBI was a mere bystander, allowing the CET1 ratio of YES
BANK to drop to an astonishing low of 0.6% while the business of YES
BANK was being carried out in a clandestine manner. It cannot be
denied that material irregularities in functioning of YES BANK were
noticed much prior; criminal prosecution has also been initiated
against the personnel of YES BANK. However, to have the investors at
the receiving end of the administrative lapses would be highly unfair.
79. We also note that the Master Circular specifies the classes of investors
to whom AT1 instruments may be offered including, among others,

34
mutual funds and insurance companies. The AT-1 Bonds are high-risk
securities and thus, as per the RBI, must be offered only to institutional
investors. However, we find that YES BANK not only permitted but
actively offered these instruments to individual investors in violation
of the Master Circular. SEBI, in its counter affidavit, has stated that the
bonds which were traded on BSE and NSE platforms were in
compliance with the relevant SEBI regulations. In fact, SEBI also
imposed penalty on a private wealth management firm as well as on
the then Managing Director of YES BANK for facilitating sale of the bonds
to private individual investors. However, the bonds which were offered
directly by YES BANK to individual investors were beyond the purview
of SEBI Regulations. An email dated 28th December, 2016, has been
placed on record by the party in person before us, seemingly
addressed by the Senior Manager - Financial Advisor of YES BANK,
Chennai offering for sale the bonds to the individual investors. Many a
bank has been hauled up by the regulator for offering such bonds to
individual investors without necessary risk disclosures. A tighter
scrutiny ought to have been exercised before luring individual investors
to such high-risk securities.
IV. CONCLUSION
80. Accordingly, for the foregoing reasons, we see no reason to interfere
with the impugned judgment. The appeals are dismissed. Interim
order, if any, stands vacated.

35
81. The payment of annual coupon rate shall remain unaffected by the
outcome of these appeals and must be made in terms of the
Information Memoranda.
82. Parties are left to bear their own costs.
83. It is clarified that observations made are only for the purpose of
decision on these appeals. Any pending proceeding may be taken to
its logical conclusion uninfluenced by any such observation.
